# XScientist: A Git-Like Research Protocol for Long-Running Autonomous Scientific Discovery

Jixiang Luo Email: [jixiangluo85@gmail.com](mailto:)

###### Abstract

Autonomous research systems can generate plausible papers while losing
the decisions, failed branches, and evidence needed to inspect or
continue the work. We present XScientist, a local-first, git-like
protocol that treats research state, rather than a manuscript, as the
unit of continuation. Hypotheses, experiment attempts, observations,
claims, reviews, and handoffs are represented as typed,
content-addressed objects in an exploration graph. Immutable
checkpoints, explicit negative outcomes, claim–evidence closure, replay
boundaries, and authority-aware gates make each transition inspectable
without treating a passing integrity check as scientific truth. The
protocol exports a portable Agent-Native Research Artifact (ARA) that
another agent or human can inspect, fork, verify, and extend. A
reference implementation integrates planning, execution, review, repair,
and supervised long-running operation while preserving provenance across
these stages. We evaluate the protocol with controlled
artifact-integrity workloads and matched external task pilots, keeping
native task performance separate from evidence and audit claims. The
result is an interoperability and accountability layer for long-running
autonomous science, with explicit boundaries where human judgment and
independent evaluation remain necessary.

Repository:
[https://github.com/smileformylove/XScientist](https://github.com/smileformylove/XScientist)

## 1 Introduction

Large language models now automate substantial parts of a scientific
workflow: ideation, experiment scripting, result interpretation,
manuscript drafting, and review simulation \[[1](#bib.bib1),
[2](#bib.bib2)\]. The difficult case is not a single successful run. It
is a research program that branches, fails, changes direction, and is
resumed by another agent or a human weeks later. For that setting, a
final PDF is an impoverished interface: it hides which decisions were
tried, which evidence was discarded, and which claims still depend on an
unverified step.

The systems question is how to maintain executable, inspectable research
state across those transitions. Experiment tracking and provenance
standards already preserve substantial execution context
\[[17](#bib.bib17), [19](#bib.bib19), [29](#bib.bib29)\]; research
agents also retain search trees and intermediate findings
\[[2](#bib.bib2), [39](#bib.bib39)\]. The unresolved design problem is
how these records govern the next research decision. If a mutable run
directory is the only reference, a correction can obscure its
predecessor. If claims are detached from evidence identities, later
edits can invalidate their support silently. If failed attempts are
omitted, a successor must reconstruct why alternatives were abandoned.
These failure modes motivate a common contract for research objects,
transitions, and evidence requirements.

### 1.1 Design Principles

XScientist addresses this problem with a git-like research protocol. The
system is designed around four principles:

1.  1.  Each research stage should emit structured artifacts that can be
        inspected without replaying the entire workflow.
2.  2.  Research state should support continuation from a specific
        experiment node instead of requiring reconstruction from the final
        PDF.
3.  3.  Manuscript assertions should remain linked to the experiment nodes
        and evidence artifacts that support them.
4.  4.  Failed branches, reviewer objections, integrity warnings, and
        blocked gates should remain first-class outputs rather than hidden
        pipeline noise.

The resulting system can run as a local project runner, a continuous
paper generator, or a daemon, but its primary output is not prose. It is
a typed, content-addressed history in which hypotheses, experiment
attempts, observations, claims, reviews, and handoffs form an
exploration graph. A portable Agent-Native Research Artifact (ARA)
exports that history for another agent or reviewer.

### 1.2 Contributions

Our central thesis is that long-running autonomous science should
promote research state, rather than a manuscript, as the unit of
continuation and audit. We make three contributions:

1.  1.  Research VCS gives scientific objects typed transitions, immutable
        checkpoints, explicit negative results, and claim–evidence closure
        rules that ordinary file history does not provide.
2.  2.  ARA packages the exploration graph, provenance, executable inputs,
        and diagnostic outcomes so that a downstream agent can fork a
        recorded node without reverse-engineering a final paper.
3.  3.  On real computational artifacts, we compare protocol checks with
        ordinary Git, complete byte hashes, and normalized JSON hashing
        under a fixed corruption matrix. The study measures auditability and
        replay boundaries; it does not claim superior scientific discovery
        or a higher benchmark score.

This framing determines how we evaluate the system. The prespecified
endpoints are per-fault rejection counts and intact-control false
rejections. A post hoc comparison examines storage baselines and the
presence of diagnostic context. Published autonomous-science benchmark
scores remain separate endpoints that require matched agents, budgets,
and independent evaluators; no such score is inferred from the artifact
study.

This separation is necessary because autonomous-science systems are
evaluated at several incompatible levels. A paper-generation study may
report reviewer ratings, a code-search system may report task success,
and a laboratory system may report human judgments or domain
measurements. Even when two systems use the same benchmark, model
version, tool access, search budget, validation protocol, intervention
policy, and treatment of failed or timed-out runs can differ. A single
aggregate score therefore risks measuring the evaluation protocol rather
than the research capability. We use matched task pilots only where the
task contract and official evaluator can be held fixed, and keep
artifact integrity, scientific-task performance, and human certification
as separate claims.

## 2 Related Work

### 2.1 Autonomous-science systems and evaluation

The AI Scientist introduced an end-to-end loop for automated idea
generation, experiment execution, paper writing, and review
\[[1](#bib.bib1)\]; related open research prototypes such as
autoresearch also explore lightweight automation loops for scientific
work \[[5](#bib.bib5)\]. AI Scientist-v2 extends this line with agentic
tree search and workshop-level paper generation \[[2](#bib.bib2)\].
XScientist follows the same broad goal of automating research workflows,
but shifts the main abstraction from “generate a paper” to “produce a
forkable research protocol artifact.” The protocol layer is intended to
make continuation, review, and cross-system handoff explicit. Parts of
the execution, tree-search, writing, and review runtime are modified
derivatives of AI-Scientist-v2, with transitive AIDE lineage. These
components are inherited foundations, not new algorithms introduced by
this paper; the additions described here concern research-state
semantics, artifact exchange, and governance.

The published systems report different endpoints and should not be
collapsed into one leaderboard. The AI Scientist reports 38 completed
diffusion papers from 51 ideas with Claude Sonnet 3.5, with a mean
automated reviewer score of 3.82 on the NeurIPS 2–6 scale (maximum 6.0);
its separate calibrated GPT-4o reviewer benchmark uses 500 ICLR 2022
papers and reports 0.65 +/- 0.04 balanced accuracy (95% bootstrap CI)
\[[1](#bib.bib1)\]. AI Scientist-v2 replaces the fixed experiment
template with a staged best-first tree search. In its reported ICLR 2025
ICBINB workshop study with 43 total submissions, three selected
AI-generated manuscripts received one acceptance decision; the accepted
manuscript’s three-reviewer mean was 6.33/10 (6, 6, 7), but it was
withdrawn before publication. This is not an unbiased 1/3 autonomous
success rate \[[2](#bib.bib2)\]. AIDE treats machine-learning
engineering as search over executable code and reports performance above
the human median on 8/16 Weco-Kaggle Lite tasks; its Table 3
reproduction of MLE-bench reports 16.9 +/- 1.1 percentage points
any-medal pass@1 for AIDE with o1-preview over 75 competitions (mean +/-
one standard error over 16 seeds) \[[6](#bib.bib6), [30](#bib.bib30)\].

Agent Laboratory adds role-specialized literature review,
experimentation, report writing, and optional human checkpoints. Its
autonomous quality study contains 15 papers; the reported human
experimental-quality means are 2.6/5 (gpt-4o), 3.2/5 (o1-mini), and
2.9/5 (o1-preview) \[[3](#bib.bib3)\]. AgentRxiv extends this workflow
with a shared archive of prior reports. In its MATH-500 study, one
sequential laboratory uses gpt-4o-mini for experiments and 40
generations, improving a 70.2% baseline to the best observed 78.2% while
retrieving five prior AgentRxiv papers and five arXiv papers; three
parallel laboratories (40 generations each) report 79.8% best accuracy
\[[4](#bib.bib4)\]. These results concern generated research quality or
task accuracy, whereas this paper evaluates whether stored research
artifacts remain checkable after corruption and replay. We therefore
report the published numbers for context, not as head-to-head evidence,
and do not claim to outperform these systems.

The comparison is intentionally separated from a discovery leaderboard.
We use four axes: end-to-end scientific-task outcome, validation-layer
ablations on a fixed run, native artifact-audit evidence, and
long-horizon recovery. The cited systems report results mainly on the
first axis. XScientist evaluates the second and third axes on fixed
artifacts and does not evaluate recovery. “NR in the cited version”
means that a paper does not report that endpoint; it is not evidence
that the system cannot support it. A future common executable-task
adapter could compare open implementations under matched models, seeds,
inputs, and budgets, but that would not be a shared scientific-discovery
score.

Two newer systems broaden the comparison beyond code and report
generation. Co-Scientist uses a multi-agent hypothesis-generation and
tournament-evolution loop with human research objectives and biomedical
validation; its Nature report describes preliminary cell-viability
inhibition for three of five expert-selected candidate compounds,
screened using four AML cell lines and a TK6 control, with three
biologically independent dose-response experiments \[[38](#bib.bib38)\].
Kosmos maintains a structured world model of research summaries, with
report statements and figures linked to publications or Jupyter
notebooks. Expert assessment of 102 statements from three representative
reports found 79.4% statement accuracy \[[39](#bib.bib39)\]. These are
domain outcomes and claim-audit measurements, not artifact-integrity
benchmarks. They further motivate XScientist’s separation between a
durable research record and a scientific claim that still requires
domain review.

Other recent proposals broaden the design space with chain-of-evidence
records, human–agent feedback, progressive discovery, autonomous
innovation, mathematical discovery, or reflective search, including
ScientistOne, AutoResearchClaw, DeepScientist, AI-Researcher, FAR, and
MARS \[[40](#bib.bib40), [41](#bib.bib41), [42](#bib.bib42),
[43](#bib.bib43), [44](#bib.bib44), [45](#bib.bib45)\]. We cite these
systems as adjacent designs; none is rerun or scored in the present
artifact-integrity study.

The comparison is therefore made on explicit axes rather than on a
single leaderboard: end-to-end scientific-task outcome, continuity of
research state, claim–evidence grounding, replay and recovery, and human
handoff. The cited systems provide useful task execution, search,
review, or memory mechanisms, but their reported artifacts do not define
a common protocol for all five axes. No external autonomous agent is
rerun here. The matched quantitative comparison in
Section [5](#S5 "5 Experimental Evaluation ‣ XScientist: A Git-Like Research Protocol for Long-Running Autonomous Scientific Discovery")
uses the same XScientist artifacts and mutations for protocol checks and
storage baselines; the source-audited capability inventory and benchmark
status are provided in the repository review archive and in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E External Benchmark Readiness ‣ XScientist: A Git-Like Research Protocol for Long-Running Autonomous Scientific Discovery").

### 2.2 Agent execution, tracking, and provenance

ReAct combines reasoning and acting in language models
\[[7](#bib.bib7)\]; Reflexion studies verbal feedback loops for language
agents \[[8](#bib.bib8)\]; Tree of Thoughts explores deliberate
branching search \[[9](#bib.bib9)\]; Voyager demonstrates open-ended
skill accumulation in an embodied environment \[[12](#bib.bib12)\].
Software-engineering agents such as SWE-agent show how interface design
affects autonomous repair \[[10](#bib.bib10)\]; AIDE explores code-space
search for ML engineering tasks \[[6](#bib.bib6)\], and AutoGen supports
multi-agent orchestration \[[11](#bib.bib11)\]. XScientist applies this
branching and repair mindset to scientific artifact management.

Long-term agent memory is a related but distinct layer. Generative
Agents maintains a memory stream with retrieval and reflection for
interactive behavior \[[13](#bib.bib13)\]; MemGPT treats context
management as an explicit hierarchy between working memory and external
storage \[[14](#bib.bib14)\]; and MemoryBank studies retrieval and
updating of long-term memories for dialogue agents \[[15](#bib.bib15)\].
TeleMem extends this line to long-term and multimodal memory with
narrative extraction and structured memory consolidation
\[[16](#bib.bib16)\]. These systems preserve useful context across
interactions, whereas XScientist preserves typed research transitions,
content-addressed evidence, failed branches, and authority-bound gates.
A memory store can help an agent remember what happened; it does not by
itself establish which recorded state is authoritative or whether a
scientific claim is replayable.

MLflow and DVC are representative tools for machine-learning lifecycle
tracking and data/model versioning \[[17](#bib.bib17),
[18](#bib.bib18)\]. They address important parts of reproducibility.
DataLad directly addresses the joint management of code, data, and their
relationships using versioned datasets \[[19](#bib.bib19)\]. Git’s
objects, trees, commits, and references provide an established model for
content identity and version history \[[20](#bib.bib20)\]. XScientist
builds on these ideas: its distinguishing design choices are the typed
research-state transitions, claim/evidence closure rules, and authority
conditions imposed on those records. File versioning, content
addressing, and preservation of execution provenance are not new
contributions of this paper. The experiment in
Section [5](#S5 "5 Experimental Evaluation ‣ XScientist: A Git-Like Research Protocol for Long-Running Autonomous Scientific Discovery")
includes ordinary Git and a whole-directory hash manifest as baselines
for byte changes.

Snakemake and Nextflow provide mature approaches to executable
computational workflows \[[21](#bib.bib21), [22](#bib.bib22)\]. Sandve
et al. recommend preserving exact inputs and programs and connecting
textual statements to underlying results \[[23](#bib.bib23)\]; the
latter anticipates an important motivation for claim anchors. The FAIR
principles address findability, accessibility, interoperability, and
reuse of research data and metadata \[[24](#bib.bib24)\]. These
principles motivate the use of explicit provenance and portable records,
but an ARA export by itself does not establish FAIR compliance,
statistical validity, or independent reproducibility.

PROV-DM models entities, activities, and agents and their provenance
relations \[[27](#bib.bib27)\]; RO-Crate packages research artifacts
with machine-readable metadata \[[28](#bib.bib28)\]. Workflow Run
RO-Crate extends this approach to workflow executions, with profiles for
inputs, outputs, code, and finer-grained execution provenance across
workflow systems \[[29](#bib.bib29)\]. Its reported applications also
include re-execution and human-review records. Portable run packaging,
layered provenance, and recording review are therefore established
capabilities. ARA is a concrete format within XScientist, coupled to its
research transitions and policy gates; it is not proposed as the first
format for those broader capabilities. This implementation has no
validated mapping to Workflow Run RO-Crate, PROV-DM, or arbitrary
third-party histories. Cross-system interoperability remains to be
demonstrated with independent producers, consumers, and explicit
preservation of policy semantics.

### 2.3 Review, integrity, and benchmark comparison

Reviewer-oriented systems such as DeepReviewer explore stronger
automated review signals \[[25](#bib.bib25)\]. Anti-Autoresearch
motivates evidence-led scrutiny of generated research artifacts
\[[26](#bib.bib26)\]. XScientist integrates reviewer-style repair with
deterministic integrity forensics, but keeps these checks conservative:
they are safeguards and audit aids, not proofs of scientific
correctness. This distinction is especially important for open review:
an internal LLM review, an external AI report, and qualified human
certification are different forms of evidence and must not be collapsed
into one status.

MLE-bench evaluates machine-learning engineering agents on 75 Kaggle
competitions with executable grading, while ScienceAgentBench evaluates
102 data-driven scientific tasks drawn from 44 peer-reviewed
publications \[[30](#bib.bib30), [31](#bib.bib31)\]. Those benchmarks
measure task-solving ability and execution outcomes. Our study instead
measures recorded-artifact validation and replay on a human-specified
workload; it does not establish competitive task-solving or end-to-end
discovery performance.

Several newer suites make a more defensible cross-system comparison
possible, provided that their native endpoints are kept separate.
CORE-Bench evaluates computational reproduction of 90 papers through 270
tasks at easy, medium, and hard environment levels \[[32](#bib.bib32)\];
PaperBench evaluates replication of 20 ICML papers with 8,316 rubric
leaves and a weighted replication score \[[33](#bib.bib33)\]. AIRS-Bench
provides 20 bounded research tasks with task-level objective evaluators
\[[34](#bib.bib34)\], while ResearchGym packages 39 subtasks from five
recent papers into longer hypothesis–experiment loops
\[[35](#bib.bib35)\]. AstaBench provides a broader suite spanning
literature, code, data analysis, and end-to-end discovery, but its
sub-benchmarks use different programmatic and LLM-based judges
\[[36](#bib.bib36)\]. RE-Bench supplies an eight-hour ML
research-engineering track with a measured expert reference
\[[37](#bib.bib37)\]. These suites are complementary: none should be
treated as a universal autonomous-discovery score, and a benchmark
result must not be combined with the artifact-integrity results reported
here.

The difficulty is not only that the suites use different tasks.
Autonomous research systems differ in model access, tool permissions,
search depth, human intervention, stopping rules, retry budgets, and the
way failed or incomplete runs enter the denominator. A reported
paper-quality score, task-success rate, wet-lab outcome, and
artifact-audit signal therefore answer different questions. A fair
horizontal comparison must freeze the task and data contract, model and
budget, tool and network access, evaluator, and failure accounting for
every arm. We follow this rule in the bounded pilots below and treat
published results as contextual evidence rather than a pooled ranking.

## 3 The XScientist Protocol

Figure
[1](#S3.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 3 The XScientist Protocol ‣ XScientist: A Git-Like Research Protocol for Long-Running Autonomous Scientific Discovery")
summarizes three logical planes. The control plane budgets, schedules,
and interrupts work. The research loop proposes experiments, executes
code, and drafts manuscripts. The artifact and verification plane
records evidence and decisions and checks the conditions for
continuation or promotion. These are logical responsibilities within a
local application, not a kernel or distributed operating system. A
manuscript is a view over this state, rather than its only source of
truth.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 1: XScientist research protocol flowchart. The upper control
plane schedules sources and budgets, the middle loop performs scientific
work, and the lower artifact plane records evidence, gates, repairs, and
provenance for later audit or forked continuation. Dashed edges denote
long-horizon feedback.

### 3.1 Execution and Artifact Model

XScientist supports individual projects, batch generation, and
long-running daemon operation through a shared artifact model. Each mode
writes structured JSON and Markdown records of ideas, research plans,
experiments, reviewer findings, repairs, manuscript candidates, quality
and integrity checks, source provenance, and handoffs. These records
provide a stable interface for agents and humans to inspect and continue
the work across execution modes.

The workflow begins by converting topics and source queues into ranked
ideas and plans that specify tasks, expected outputs, baselines,
acceptance checks, and execution policies. A tree-search-style
experiment loop then records code, stdout/stderr, metrics, plots, and
failure states. Failed branches remain available to explain subsequent
repairs, softened claims, or decisions to stop a branch. The writing
layer produces manuscript candidates and structured metadata; text and
figure review identify issues and schedule repairs using novelty, rigor,
clarity, and reproducibility criteria. Management views expose the
resulting papers, unresolved issues, and repair priorities to operators.

Research VCS records this workflow as typed objects and checkpoints. A
checkpoint can add a question, hypothesis, experiment attempt,
observation, evidence item, claim, review, reproduction, or gate
decision, together with content hashes, actor and environment receipts,
and explicit negative outcomes. ARA is the portable export of one run,
while Research VCS provides the append-only history for comparing
multiple runs, branches, and semantic corrections. Mutable working state
and refs remain separate from immutable objects and checkpoints;
corrections create new objects linked by supersedes or use a typed
revert checkpoint.

Execution is governed by explicit budgets and review boundaries. The
policy engine distinguishes local syntax and integrity checks from
replay and independent verification: passing a local check does not
establish scientific truth. A research cycle need not advance to a full
manuscript. A failed sample gate, a violated truth contract, a hard
integrity flag, or an operator pause can stop the run, and these
stopping states are retained as valid outcomes.

### 3.2 Typed History, Branches, and Corrections

The Research VCS is the repository-level protocol that gives the paper’s
“git-like” analogy precise meaning. It is not a wrapper around ordinary
Git commands. Git may provide storage, but the scientific semantics are
defined by typed research objects, content-addressed identities,
checkpoint-parent relations, refs, and policy validation.

The object vocabulary covers the stages that reviewers need to inspect:
questions and search plans, source snapshots and passage evidence,
hypotheses, preregistrations, experiment attempts, observations,
metrics, evidence, claims, reviews, gate decisions, manuscripts,
reproductions, and agent evaluations. Objects carry a schema identifier,
lifecycle state, typed relations, actor and provenance fields, and a
canonical content hash. Some fields may be empty in lightweight records;
stronger closure profiles require the corresponding evidence and
receipts.

An ordinary checkpoint can add objects or record a semantic correction,
but it cannot overwrite an existing object. A correction creates a new
object linked with supersedes; a rollback creates a checkpoint binding
the commit and checkpoint hash being reverted. Failed, timed-out,
cancelled, negative, contradictory, and rejected attempts, when recorded
and committed, remain inspectable in the reachable checkpoint history.
This does not recover events never recorded or preserve an unmerged
branch whose only ref was removed. Append-only semantics are enforced
through the protocol API; direct backend access remains within the
operator’s trust boundary.

### 3.3 Evidence Closure and Authority Boundaries

Schema validation constrains representation, while integrity checks test
consistency with declared identities. Separately, the closure auditor
reports trace, replay, and verify: trace checks the recorded
claim/evidence lineage; replay checks that required execution
prerequisites are represented; verify adds the required review, gate,
and reproduction records. A replay_ready status is not evidence of a
successful execution. Actual re-execution produces a separate report,
evaluated against an explicit metric and tolerance.

A matching hash establishes consistency with the recorded content, not
that an event occurred or that a measurement is scientifically valid.
The local implementation can verify Ed25519 signatures and bind receipts
to evidence; establishing the external trust root, evaluator
independence, and appropriate domain expertise remains a deployment
responsibility.

The publication-oriented profile requires confirmatory and reproduction
records to bind the relevant evidence, producers, evaluators, and
attempt dispositions. Other profiles and legacy records can be less
complete. A claim can be descriptive without being causal or
transferable; stronger statuses require stronger evidence and
independent gates. The implementation intentionally fails closed when a
required link is absent instead of inferring completion from prose or
model self-assessment.

#### 3.3.1 Portable History and Scientific Conflicts

ARA and Research VCS solve adjacent problems. ARA is a portable export
for one end-to-end run, suitable for copying to an issue, archive, or
another agent. Research VCS is the durable history across runs, with
named branches, semantic diffs, merges, blame, policy decisions, and
reproduction receipts. The project runner projects ARA evidence and
claim references into Research VCS and binds the manifest and
exploration-graph hashes. This is a specific bridge, not a lossless
import of arbitrary third-party research histories. Projected claims
remain drafts until the required gates are satisfied.

Two branches may contain byte-compatible files yet support incompatible
scientific interpretations. Research relations therefore distinguish
supports, refutes, contradicts, depends_on, and supersedes. A merge
records the selected resolution policy; it cannot establish truth by
choosing the last writer or the largest metric. Comparable branches
additionally need aligned task, dataset split, metric, budget, and
evaluator definitions. Preserving both branches exposes disagreement but
does not resolve it scientifically.

The checkpoint-parent DAG supplies causal ordering for the recorded
history. Timestamps are provenance metadata and do not establish that
preregistration preceded execution or that an evaluator was independent.
Confirmatory publication uses stronger state and authority bindings.
This separation is central to the Git analogy: a commit identifies a
research transition, while accepting its scientific interpretation
remains an evidence-dependent act.

### 3.4 Portable Artifacts and Continuation

The run-level exchange interface is the Agent-Native Research Artifact
(ARA). An ARA is a directory rooted at a manifest.json file and an
exploration_graph.json file. It is designed to be read by another agent
without requiring that agent to reverse-engineer the final paper.

#### 3.4.1 Exploration DAG

Each ARA stores an exploration DAG whose nodes represent exported
experiment states, including repair, failure, and ablation states when
those states were recorded by the producer. Edges encode the
parent-to-child evolution of the run. Manuscript candidates and related
pipeline artifacts can be retained as separate records; they are not
necessarily experiment nodes. The validator checks node identity, edge
endpoints, counts, and acyclicity. The producer can also write a summary
and a self-contained HTML visualization.

The exploration DAG is intentionally not a polished success-only
lineage. It includes bug states, discarded branches, and repaired
branches because those states are often the most important for later
review. A downstream agent that sees only the final successful
experiment cannot know whether the result was robust, whether a metric
was changed midstream, or whether a failed baseline was silently
dropped. ARA makes those transitions inspectable.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 2: Conceptual science exploration DAG. ARA preserves recorded
successful and failed branches, allowing later agents to audit or fork a
specific node. The manuscript and claim records shown here are relations
and derived views; they need not be experiment nodes in every export.

#### 3.4.2 Identity, Claims, and Operational Views

ARA uses content hashes to identify node payloads and manifest
revisions. Current producers use the ara.node-identity.v2 profile, which
binds a SHA-256 digest of the complete stripped UTF-8 source, normalized
metric fields, and declared extra references such as context or
execution receipts. Consumers retain legacy identity support rather than
silently reinterpreting old artifacts. Forked runs preserve parent
pointers, so a child run can identify the earlier ARA and node that
seeded it. These hashes establish local content integrity, not the truth
of a measurement or the independence of its producer. ARA node
identities retain their own serialization profile for compatibility.
Newer trust-boundary commitments use the stricter
xscientist.canonical-json.v1 profile, with Python and JavaScript
conformance fixtures. Those fixtures exercise that separate byte-level
boundary; they do not establish cross-language ARA node-identity
conformance or a second complete protocol implementation.

In practice, this gives XScientist a commit-like substrate. The final
PDF is only one rendered view. The underlying research state can be
diffed, logged, forked, or frozen. When an ARA is committed to a normal
git repository, git records file-level snapshots, while ARA commands
expose node-level scientific history inside those snapshots.

Generated manuscripts can include invisible \claimref markers after
quantitative or evidence-sensitive claims. A claim registry scans the
source and writes the resolved or unresolved claim records under the
ARA. The marker is a pointer, not a judgment that the cited node entails
the claim. Coverage and resolution status can be summarized for quality
gates and downstream reviewers; missing or unresolved anchors remain
explicit.

The installed CLI xscientist ara exposes operational verbs: inspect,
exec, fork, freeze, validate, verify, diff, log, and refs. These
commands let an operator inspect a node, re-execute its code, create a
new seed ARA, compare two ARAs, or walk the provenance chain. The same
graph data underlies the HTML visualization, the log view, and
node-level diffs.

#### 3.4.3 Portable Exchange

The base ara.v1 contract requires two files: manifest.json and
exploration_graph.json. Optional but common files include per-node
code.py, term_out.log, metrics.json, plots.json, environment snapshots,
claim records, verification reports, repair history, Pareto candidate
pools, and a human-facing HTML graph view. Legacy producers may declare
absent optional artifacts in manifest.missing. This does not waive the
requirements of stronger profiles: an authority-bound run also requires
its attempt index, referenced content-addressed object, and portable
authority ledgers. Missing or invalid required records cause validation
to fail.

The complete directory contract is provided in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B ARA Directory Contract ‣ XScientist: A Git-Like Research Protocol for Long-Running Autonomous Scientific Discovery");
the main text keeps the protocol invariant rather than a file inventory.

ARA uses ordinary files so that an export can be copied, archived,
attached to an issue, reviewed in a pull request, or consumed by another
agent without running an XScientist service. Databases and object stores
remain useful backends for querying or scale; the protocol keeps the
portable boundary independent of those services. As in software
repositories, different tools can provide richer views over the same
explicitly versioned state.

Autonomous research systems require checks that are deterministic enough
to be run in CI and explicit enough to be audited later. XScientist
implements several such controls.

### 3.5 Review, Repair, and Integrity Controls

The self-review subsystem runs LLM-based and VLM-assisted reviews,
extracts structured issues, prioritizes repairs, and records repair
attempts. The system tracks whether reviewer objections were addressed,
whether manuscript changes regressed earlier claims, and whether quality
thresholds were met.

Repair is represented as a trace rather than as a single overwrite. The
system records which issue motivated a repair, which artifact was
modified, which checks were rerun, and whether the repair introduced new
risks. This is important for generated manuscripts because a fluent
rewrite can hide evidence loss. XScientist therefore treats repair
coverage and regression detection as first-class quality signals.

#### 3.5.1 Quality and Integrity Gates

Truth contracts translate a research plan into explicit constraints.
They separate objective facts, comparability constraints,
artifact-binding rules, branch-state rules, and value guardrails. For
example, a manuscript should not claim a baseline-comparable improvement
unless the experiment registry contains a completed run on the declared
dataset, metric, and baseline.

The categories are intentionally broad: objective facts, comparability
constraints, artifact-binding rules, branch-state transitions, and value
guardrails. They are not a formal proof system. They are a pragmatic
checklist that converts ambiguous planner intent into concrete
conditions that can be checked later by gates, reviewers, or downstream
agents.

Before full generation, sample gates can require that a small planned
task has a completed experiment record, a budget audit, passing
acceptance checks, and a result summary. This prevents the system from
scaling a flawed plan into a full paper when the cheap preliminary
evidence is missing.

XScientist adapts an evidence-ledger pattern inspired by
Anti-Autoresearch into the manuscript stage. The integrity forensics
pass is not an authorship detector. It builds a span-anchored ledger
from the manuscript source, applies model-free consistency checks, and
writes a deterministic adjudication report. Hard findings can block
submission-ready status; soft findings are reported for reviewer
attention.

The deterministic design is deliberate. Model-based critique is useful,
but a submission gate needs repeatable behavior. Integrity forensics
therefore focuses on checks that can be rerun with the same result:
suspicious pipeline artifacts in the manuscript, unsupported strong
wording, arithmetic drift in reported deltas, citation placeholders,
repeated caption/table presentation signals, and evidence-ledger gaps.
It is a conservative screen for risks that deserve attention before a
paper is treated as submission-ready. Passing the screen does not
establish citation entailment, statistical validity, data provenance, or
scientific truth; false negatives and false positives remain possible
and require human adjudication.

Recent XScientist runs also write decision logs for workflow strategy,
sample-gate outcomes, and model-provider choices. Gate preconditions are
checked before expensive or high-risk stages proceed. For example, a
quality gate that requires high-quality mode should not run under a
cheaper classic pipeline by accident; a full-generation stage should not
proceed when the sample gate is blocked. These checks turn implicit
workflow assumptions into explicit runtime contracts.

| Control             | Signal                                                     | Effect                                                                 |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Sample gate         | Sample task completion, budget audit, acceptance checks    | Blocks full generation when cheap preliminary evidence is absent.      |
| Truth contract      | Plan-derived facts, comparability rules, artifact bindings | Checks registered facts and comparability conditions before promotion. |
| Integrity forensics | Span ledger, deterministic consistency checks              | Raises hard or soft manuscript risk flags.                             |
| Review repair trace | Structured issues, repair attempts, regression checks      | Shows how reviewer objections were addressed.                          |
| Gate preconditions  | Workflow mode, quality mode, gate requirements             | Stops incompatible stage combinations before expensive execution.      |

Table 1: Quality controls in XScientist. The goal is not to prove
correctness automatically, but to make risk states explicit and
reproducible.

## 4 Implementation and Operation

The daemon mode treats research as an ongoing operation rather than a
single script invocation. It supports source queues, source health
tracking, dashboard serving, daily reports, handoff briefs, pause/resume
controls, source boosting and cooldown, failure protection, and strategy
feedback.

Operational state accumulates across cycles. Source health, blocked
gates, remaining budget, and pending review actions inform subsequent
scheduling. The scheduler records these signals and control decisions.
This capability supports long-running operation; its effect on
scientific productivity and multi-day reliability is not evaluated in
this paper.

### 4.1 Supervised Operation

The daemon is designed for supervised autonomy. Operators can pause and
resume, stop after the current cycle, force or boost a source, apply a
cooldown, inspect dashboard state, and generate handoff reports. This
makes the system suitable for long-running local operation where full
automation is not always desirable. A useful autonomous research system
should make it easy to interrupt, inspect, and redirect.

The daemon collects feedback at several levels: paper-level quality
signals, source-level health, strategy-level success rates, repair
pressure, and process alignment. These signals can influence later
scheduling and execution policy. For example, a source that repeatedly
produces blocked sample gates can be cooled down, while a source
producing useful review-hardening tasks can be boosted when a manuscript
is near submission.

### 4.2 Reproducibility and Release

XScientist separates implementation code from a user-selected research
workspace. The output location is configuration-dependent and should be
recorded explicitly. For reproducibility, a report should cite the
public repository, configuration, model choices, output directory, and
the ARA root used for any generated paper. For the present system
report, the canonical repository is
[https://github.com/smileformylove/XScientist](https://github.com/smileformylove/XScientist).

The recommended release workflow for a generated manuscript is:

1.  1.  run the project or daemon under an explicit output root and budget;
2.  2.  inspect the generated manuscript, ARA, review reports, and integrity
        forensics;
3.  3.  verify or re-execute important ARA nodes where feasible;
4.  4.  check claim coverage and manually review evidence-sensitive claims;
5.  5.  package the manuscript and artifact references with the review
        archive.

This workflow does not guarantee correctness, but it raises the cost of
silent evidence loss and makes later review more concrete.

## 5 Experimental Evaluation

The evaluation tests the paper’s central claim at the artifact boundary.
We ask whether the protocol (i) preserves a replayable record from real
computation, (ii) distinguishes different classes of inconsistency, and
(iii) gives a reviewer more specific evidence than a changed-file
signal. A fourth question compares those outcomes with ordinary Git and
complete byte hashing, including serialization changes that preserve
parsed JSON values. These are mechanism questions, not a proxy for
autonomous-discovery quality.

The study uses 20 real executions on the public Breast Cancer Wisconsin
dataset \[[46](#bib.bib46), [47](#bib.bib47)\], producing 20 intact
ARAs. Each is copied into six fixed single-fault variants (changed code,
changed metric, graph cycle, dangling endpoint, missing code, and
invalid schema type), yielding 120 paired fixtures. The primary
endpoints are per-fault rejection counts (out of 20 paired variants) and
rejection of intact controls (out of 20); fault-class coverage in
Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5.1 Results ‣ 5 Experimental Evaluation ‣ XScientist: A Git-Like Research Protocol for Long-Running Autonomous Scientific Discovery")
and
Table [5](#S5.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 5.1 Results ‣ 5 Experimental Evaluation ‣ XScientist: A Git-Like Research Protocol for Long-Running Autonomous Scientific Discovery")
is a derived summary requiring all 20 variants in a class to be
rejected. A later post hoc audit additionally counted whether saved
reports contained a non-empty reason and location; this records signal
presence, not diagnostic accuracy. The complete protocol, environment,
hashes, and per-package reports appear in the repository review archive.

The quantitative baselines are whole-directory SHA-256, plain Git, and a
normalized-JSON hash that canonicalizes JSON object order and
whitespace. They operate on the same saved packages and use an
externally retained intact reference, whereas XScientist’s integrity
check uses identities declared in the candidate package. This difference
in custody is part of the comparison. For external task performance we
report a common-schedule AIRS-Bench SICK generated-program study, a
matched ten-task ScienceAgentBench subset, a 20-item public-data LitQA2
scorer pilot from the AstaBench family, and a CORE-Bench Hard
preparation in which a five-capsule manifest was frozen but only one
exploratory capsule was executed. All are named as bounded feasibility
studies rather than full-suite or leaderboard results. Other public
suites and their unfulfilled hardware or data contracts are documented
in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E External Benchmark Readiness ‣ XScientist: A Git-Like Research Protocol for Long-Running Autonomous Scientific Discovery")

Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5.1 Results ‣ 5 Experimental Evaluation ‣ XScientist: A Git-Like Research Protocol for Long-Running Autonomous Scientific Discovery")
and
Table [5](#S5.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 5.1 Results ‣ 5 Experimental Evaluation ‣ XScientist: A Git-Like Research Protocol for Long-Running Autonomous Scientific Discovery")

replay adds executable evidence but no additional rejection on this
targeted set. These are paired fixture outcomes, not estimates of
natural fault prevalence or scientific validity.

Two misses clarify the boundaries. Appending an extra print statement
changes the source bytes but leaves balanced accuracy unchanged, so
metric replay accepts it and the content check rejects it. Conversely,
adding a graph cycle or dangling endpoint leaves the selected node’s
code and metric unchanged; the tested node-hash/manifest-lock check and
single-node replay accept these packages, whereas structural validation
rejects them. This is why none of these checks alone is an adequate
proxy for the others.

### 5.2 Additional Storage Baselines and Representation Controls

The storage comparison asks whether this coverage is simply a
consequence of checking bytes. Whole-directory SHA-256 and plain Git
match the combined protocol on the six selected fault classes and on the
intact controls. A normalized-JSON hash also accepts the
representation-preserving rewrites, whereas byte-level baselines flag
them. Thus the experiment does not show a detection advantage for
XScientist or a unique serialization invariant. The measured difference
is semantic: protocol reports retain the violated relation, typed field,
or metric identity (for example, a self-loop at edges\[0\]), while
storage comparators report changed paths. The
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Comparator Definitions ‣ XScientist: A Git-Like Research Protocol for Long-Running Autonomous Scientific Discovery")
contains the exact comparator rules and
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Diagnostic Examples ‣ XScientist: A Git-Like Research Protocol for Long-Running Autonomous Scientific Discovery")
contains diagnostic examples; the signal-presence count is not a claim
of root-cause accuracy or reviewer benefit.

### 5.3 Interpretation and Scope

The computational workload establishes that the packages contain metrics
computed from real predictions and reproducible commands. The relevant
systems result is the combination of fault-class coverage,
intact-control acceptance, and protocol diagnostic context. Schema
checks constrain representation; graph checks add relational invariants;
hashes check consistency with declared identities or reference bytes;
replay compares a declared metric under a recorded command. A combined
pass on a valid control is not an independent reproduction or a
scientific endorsement.

The workloads do not exercise autonomous hypothesis generation,
multi-day daemon reliability, or human review quality, and the native
agent comparisons are bounded CPU pilots rather than full discovery
evaluations against AI-Scientist-v2 or AIDE. They also do not measure
the rate of naturally occurring corruption. Those questions require
matched tasks, budgets, prospective runs, independent evaluators, and
domain-appropriate outcomes. The bundled demonstration’s prewritten
retrieval rates are synthetic examples and are excluded from every
empirical table in this paper.

## 6 Discussion and Limitations

XScientist does not make autonomous research automatically correct. The
system can organize evidence, preserve provenance, and expose warnings,
but human review remains necessary for scientific validity, ethical
judgment, and final submission decisions. The current system also has
several engineering limitations:

- •
  Re-execution can be expensive or environment-dependent when nodes call
  external APIs, GPUs, or web services.
- •
  Integrity forensics is deterministic but incomplete; its
  false-positive and false-negative rates on naturally occurring
  manuscripts have not been measured in this study.
- •
  ARA is a protocol surface rather than a universal standard; broader
  adoption requires independent producers and consumers.
- •
  The daemon provides operational controls, but no multi-day endurance
  or crash-recovery comparison is reported here. Long-running autonomy
  still needs explicit budgets, stop conditions, and operator oversight.
- •
  The present paper is a system report. It documents the implementation
  and protocol surface with a narrow computational evaluation. It does
  not provide a controlled user study, human-versus-agent comparison, or
  a broad external discovery benchmark.

### 6.1 Internal and External Validity

The evaluation uses one small, well-understood dataset, simple classical
models, one platform, and author-designed faults. Multiple corrupted
copies of a package are paired test cases, not independent scientific
studies. The protocol and checker were developed in the same project,
and the local execution environment is not an independent verifier. The
evaluated commit is fixed; later changes may alter results and require a
new evaluation. The external task study is intentionally bounded. The
AIRS rows are exact official-evaluator scores on a 4,906-row held-out
SICK generated-program task, but use an adapted three-candidate CPU
schedule and one seed rather than the canonical AIRS agent protocol.
ScienceAgentBench uses a fixed ten-task verified subset and reports
$`1/10`$ for AI Scientist-v2 and $`2/10`$ for XScientist; the shared
evaluator exception is retained in both denominators. A paired
CORE-Bench retry on capsule-9052293 reached the evaluator for both arms
and scored $`0/1`$ in each, because the capsule script failed under the
pinned xlrd/Python 3.13 environment. This is a reproducibility-failure
record, not a successful task result; the earlier single-arm $`1/1`$
trajectory is retained separately. A valid full-suite comparison must
use the same agent-facing task, model, budget, seed/retry policy,
hardware, and evaluator for every system; native scores remain separate
from artifact and recovery metrics.

### 6.2 Adversary Model

The fault experiment tests inconsistencies against recorded identities.
An operator who controls source, data, records, and trust configuration
can construct a mutually consistent but fabricated history, including
recomputing hashes after changing the contents. Local content addressing
cannot prevent this. External attestations can bind a trusted verifier’s
statement to exact bytes, but cannot repair an invalid study design or
confer independence on a colluding evaluator. These risks are outside
the demonstrated detection results.

### 6.3 Ethics and Operational Safety

Autonomous research tooling can create plausible but incorrect
scientific artifacts at high speed. XScientist is therefore designed to
preserve uncertainty, not to erase it. The system records failed
branches, exposes blocked gates, and explicitly states that integrity
forensics is incomplete. Users should not submit generated papers
without human review, should disclose substantial automated assistance
when appropriate, and should avoid using the system for domains where
erroneous claims can cause direct harm without additional expert
oversight.

There is also an operational safety concern: long-running agents can
consume API credits, compute, and storage unexpectedly. XScientist
includes output isolation, preflight checks, daemon controls, and
budget-oriented gates, but operators remain responsible for configuring
limits and monitoring runs.

### 6.4 Implications

The central design claim of XScientist is that a manuscript is a
rendered view of a research history. When runs branch, fail, and resume,
the reviewable unit is the history: the state transitions, evidence
links, and decisions that justify the current view. The controlled study
supports the narrower systems claim behind this design. XScientist
matches storage baselines on the selected fault coverage, while
reporting reasons and diagnostic context tied to the protocol. The
designed continuation semantics extend this representation; their effect
on recovery cost still requires a longitudinal experiment.

The same design suggests a path toward collaborative autonomous science:
systems can exchange ARAs, fork one another’s nodes, inspect
claim/evidence links without parsing PDFs, and use git-like diffs to
review scientific changes. This is an interoperability objective that
still needs independent producers and consumers. For human review, the
immediate benefit is more concrete: a reviewer can request an exact
artifact or disputed transition, and an author response can point to a
new immutable record. A platform’s human-certification decision remains
external to XScientist’s internal gates.

## 7 Conclusion

XScientist implements a Git-like protocol for maintaining scientific
state across research runs. Research VCS records typed objects and
transitions; ARA exports run-level evidence and execution artifacts;
closure and authority checks constrain how those records can support a
claim. The controlled evaluation demonstrates complementary detection
behavior across schema, structure, content-integrity, and replay checks
on real computational artifacts. Complete hash comparison, normalized
JSON hashing, and ordinary Git match its fault coverage; the additional
JSON controls distinguish byte identity from the tested protocol
invariants. The protocol reports invariant- specific reasons and
locations for the selected faults, while the study does not establish
general autonomous discovery performance. The protocol provides an
inspectable basis for continuation and review while leaving scientific
validity and independent certification explicit.

## Availability

The primary artifact for this report is the public XScientist GitHub
repository:

[https://github.com/smileformylove/XScientist](https://github.com/smileformylove/XScientist)

It contains the implementation, ARA protocol schemas, command-line
tools, examples, documentation, and tests. The arXiv source for this
system report is maintained in the same repository under:

paper/xscientist_arxiv/

The accompanying review archive contains the evaluation protocol,
driver, raw predictions, validation reports, generated tables, and
complete evaluated source. Saved-result verification can use that
archive without fetching the source from the remote repository. The
local environment and exact dependency versions are recorded with the
run. Neither the earlier preprint nor this revision is represented as
having received human certification.

An OpenAI Codex coding assistant supported literature and source-code

execution. The computational workload and validation checks call no
language-model provider. AI-assisted drafting and internal automated
checks are not independent peer review. The named author remains
responsible for the manuscript, citations, interpretation of the
recorded results, and the declarations accompanying submission.

Anti-Autoresearch. Their published benchmark results are not inherited
by XScientist.

## Appendix A Evaluation Contract

This appendix is part of the submitted PDF and records the material
needed to interpret the mechanism study without turning the main text
into an execution log. The frozen evaluation uses 20 real computational
executions on the Breast Cancer Wisconsin (Diagnostic) data, with ten
fixed stratified splits and two fixed models per split. Each execution
exports one intact ARA. Six single fault operators are applied
independently to each ARA: source-code tampering, metric tampering, a
graph self-loop, a dangling edge endpoint, removal of the replay source,
and an invalid schema type. The resulting 120 variants are paired with
their 20 intact controls.

For a check, “rejection” means that the check rejects the predefined
fixture variant; it is not a sensitivity, precision, or security
estimate. A false rejection is rejection of an unchanged control. The
replay check uses a 60-second timeout and an absolute balanced-accuracy
tolerance of $`10^{-12}`$. An exception is recorded as a failed check
and retained with its diagnostic. The six fault classes and their
intended invariant are:

| Fault operator   | Intended invariant under test                                |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| code_tamper      | source bytes agree with the declared node identity           |
| metric_tamper    | recorded metric agrees with the declared identity and replay |
| graph_cycle      | exploration graph remains acyclic                            |
| missing_endpoint | every edge endpoint names a present node                     |
| missing_code     | replay inputs required by the node are present               |
| schema_type      | schema field types remain valid                              |

The complete protocol, source and data hashes, environment record, raw
packages, per-package reports, and generated tables are retained under
paper/xscientist_arxiv/evaluation/. The primary table in the main text
reports class coverage so that the denominator is visible without
suggesting that the paired fixtures are independent observations.

## Appendix B ARA Directory Contract

The base ara.v1 export requires the two entry-point files below.
Stronger conformance and authority profiles add mandatory records. The
file-based boundary can be archived, diffed, copied, or consumed by
tools that do not run an XScientist service.

| Artifact               | Status   | Purpose                                                                                         |
| ---------------------- | -------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| manifest.json          | required | Entry point, schema version, counts, references, provenance, and missing-artifact declarations. |
| exploration_graph.json | required | Node and edge set for the science exploration DAG.                                              |
| nodes/\<id\>/          | optional | Per-node code, metrics, logs, plots, environment descriptors, and rerun script.                 |
| claims/                | optional | Claim-to-node anchors extracted from manuscript source.                                         |
| verify/                | optional | Re-execution reports and metric-drift checks.                                                   |
| pipeline/              | optional | Mirrored planning, review, repair, and gate artifacts for downstream agents.                    |

Table 6: Base ARA directory contract. Optional artifacts may be declared
in manifest.missing; this does not waive requirements of stronger
profiles.

## Appendix C Comparator Definitions

The storage baselines use an externally retained intact package.
Whole-tree SHA-256 compares each regular file’s relative path, size, and
raw-content digest. Plain Git commits the intact package in an isolated
repository and checks tracked and untracked differences with hooks,
signing, text conversion, global attributes, and external configuration
disabled. Neither baseline interprets scientific relations.

The normalized-JSON comparator parses JSON with duplicate keys and
non-finite constants rejected, serializes object keys in sorted order
with fixed separators, and hashes the canonical bytes; non-JSON files
remain byte-hashed. It is used only for the representation controls and
the same saved fault packages. The XScientist C+I row in the audit is a
conjunction of saved conformance and integrity outcomes; it is not a new
replay run. On the selected faults, all three storage baselines and C+I
reject 120/120 variants and accept 20/20 intact controls. The normalized
comparator accepts 20/20 representation controls; byte baselines flag
those changes. These results establish matched behavior for this fixture
set, not general superiority.

## Appendix D Diagnostic Examples

The protocol report preserves an invariant-specific reason and a
location in addition to the changed path. Representative saved signals
are:

| Fault            | Representative protocol signal                     | Location                      |
| ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| Code change      | code differs from the declared node identity       | nodes/experiment/code.py      |
| Metric change    | metric differs from the declared node identity     | nodes/experiment/metrics.json |
| Self-loop        | node experiment links to itself                    | edges\[0\]                    |
| Missing endpoint | edge child absent_node is not present              | edges\[0\]                    |
| Missing code     | replay requested but the source artifact is absent | conformance                   |
| Invalid type     | counts.nodes is not an integer                     | counts.nodes                  |

Each signal is present for all 20 paired instances of its class in the
saved reports. This is a signal-presence endpoint, not a claim of
root-cause accuracy, reviewer-time reduction, or independent custody. A
self-consistent fabricated history can evade local checks if an operator
is allowed to rewrite the declared identities and trust configuration.

## Appendix E External Benchmark Readiness

The public suites below provide possible matched task endpoints. They
are listed to define the reproducible comparison contract. The per-suite
source pins, blocked conditions, and adapter commands are retained here
so that the main-table entries can be audited without duplicating the
matrix.

The archived CORE-Bench preparation uses a temporary local path
adaptation and no Docker. The five-capsule manifest is a frozen
task-selection record. A paired retry on capsule-9052293 reached the
official evaluator for both arms and returned $`0/1`$ for each after the
capsule script failed under xlrd/Python 3.13; the earlier single-arm
$`1/1`$ trajectory is retained separately and is not a paired or
leaderboard score. The AIRS adapter pins the official evaluator and uses
a separate evaluator directory/process for test-label injection; this
layout is not an OS or container security boundary. Candidate selection
may read only the public training and validation splits; the
agent-facing test split remains unlabeled until the official grader runs
after submission. A canonical comparison must fix the benchmark commit
and data hashes, model/API identifier, prompts, seed and retry policy,
tool and network access, wall-clock and token budget, hardware, output
contract, stopping rule, and evaluator version. It should publish the
benchmark’s native score beside protocol endpoints such as artifact
completeness, claim–evidence closure, replay success, failed-branch
retention, and recovery time, without averaging the two families.

The completed bounded runs are retained with their raw inputs and
evaluator outputs. The three-arm AIRS SICK study is under
external_benchmarks/airs_agent/runs/airs_sick_generated_fair_20260922/;
its held-out classification scores are 0.8127 (AIDE), 0.8047 (AI
Scientist-v2), and 0.8182 (XScientist), while similarity scores are
0.7131, 0.7219, and 0.7055. The ScienceAgentBench comparison is under
external_benchmarks/native_science/runs/sab_v2_full/ and
external_benchmarks/native_science/runs/sab_xsci_full/; its official
task-success counts are 1/10 and 2/10. The CORE-Bench preparation and
exploratory runs are under external_benchmarks/corebench_matched/; the
paired retry record reports $`0/1`$ for both arms after the capsule’s
xlrd/Python 3.13 execution failure, and the earlier protocol-only record
reports $`1/1`$ separately. Neither is a full-suite leaderboard result.
The AstaBench-family LitQA2 scorer pilot is under
external_benchmarks/api_cpu_secondary/runs/20260921_190219_litqa2_20matched/;
on 20 public LAB-Bench items, the direct GPT-5.6 arm scored $`10/20`$
and the XScientist router scored $`8/20`$. The receipt marks this result
non-canonical because the official AstaBench split mapping is gated.
These records are auditable feasibility evidence, not full-suite
leaderboard submissions.

## Appendix F Reproduction Commands

From the repository root of a clean checkout, the saved-result verifier
can be run as follows:

```ltx_verbatim
python paper/xscientist_arxiv/evaluation/verify_results.py \
  --run paper/xscientist_arxiv/evaluation/raw/run_20260919_01 \
  --repo . \
  --report verification-local.json
```

From the root of the extracted review bundle, use the bundled evaluated
source archive:

```ltx_verbatim
python manuscript/evaluation/verify_results.py \
  --run manuscript/evaluation/raw/run_20260919_01 \
  --source-archive source/xscientist-evaluated-source.tar \
  --report verification-local.json

python manuscript/evaluation/comparison_20260919/verify_comparison.py \
  --base-run manuscript/evaluation/raw/run_20260919_01 \
  --comparison-run manuscript/evaluation/comparison_20260919/run_20260919_03 \
  --source-archive source/xscientist-evaluated-source.tar
```

These commands verify saved evidence and hashes; they do not claim
external custody or independent scientific review. Re-running the full
computation requires the pinned source snapshot and dependencies
described in the evaluation archive. The benchmark adapters similarly
record source pins, submission snapshots, grader stdout/stderr, and
failure states, but an adapter smoke test is not a benchmark score.
